Flagitious
fla-jĭsh´ŭs
adj. (grossly criminal; villainous beyond the common measure)
Latin flagitiosus, from flagitium, a shameful act — related to flagitare, to demand hotly, and so originally the deed a hot passion demands.

Biblical Definition

A flagitious act is criminality of a kind that shocks even a corrupt society. God says of Sodom, “because their sin is very grievous” (Gen 18:20). Ezekiel is shown worse and worse: “turn thee yet again, and thou shalt see greater abominations” (Eze 8:6). Jeremiah reports a national condition: “A wonderful and horrible thing is committed in the land” (Jer 5:30). Paul finds in the church at Corinth “such fornication as is not so much as named among the Gentiles” (1Co 5:1). And the outrage at Gibeah draws the strongest sentence in Judges: “there was no such deed done nor seen from the day that the children of Israel came up out of the land of Egypt unto this day” (Jdg 19:30).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines flagitious as deeply criminal; grossly wicked; villainous; atrocious; and, of a person, guilty of enormous crimes.

expand to see more

FLAGITIOUS, a. Deeply criminal; grossly wicked; villainous; atrocious; scandalous; as a flagitious action or crime.

2. Guilty of enormous crimes; corrupt; wicked; as a flagitious person.

3. Very wicked; corrupt; abandoned; as flagitious times.

Key Scripture

Gen 18:20 — "And the LORD said, Because the cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great, and because their sin is very grievous;"

Eze 8:6 — "He said furthermore unto me, Son of man, seest thou what they do? even the great abominations that the house of Israel committeth here, that I should go far off from my sanctuary? but turn thee yet again, and thou shalt see greater abominations."

Jer 5:30 — "A wonderful and horrible thing is committed in the land;"

1Co 5:1 — "It is reported commonly that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not so much as named among the Gentiles, that one should have his father's wife."

Jdg 19:30 — "And it was so, that all that saw it said, There was no such deed done nor seen from the day that the children of Israel came up out of the land of Egypt unto this day: consider of it, take advice, and speak your minds."

Modern Corruption

The church expects gross wickedness outside its walls, and Paul's example is a case inside a congregation that was proud of itself.

expand to see more

First Corinthians 5:1 is the passage that should stop any congregation from locating this word entirely outside itself. There is fornication among you, Paul writes, and such fornication as is not so much as named among the Gentiles — the pagans of Corinth, a city whose morals were a byword in the ancient world, would have been shocked. And the next clause is worse: and ye are puffed up, and have not rather mourned. The congregation was proud. Not of the sin, but of a tolerance that felt like maturity, and Paul's charge is that they had not grieved.

Judges 19 is the darkest chapter in the Old Testament and the narrator does not editorialise; he lets the deed stand and records Israel's reaction: consider of it, take advice, and speak your minds. The book's refrain explains how a nation arrives there — in those days there was no king in Israel, every man did that which was right in his own eyes — and the sequence matters. Flagitious acts appear at the end of a process in which each man became his own standard, and they appear among the covenant people.

The reason to keep the category at all is that a church without it will handle grave sin as though it were ordinary, and Paul's instruction in 1 Corinthians 5 is severe precisely because the case was. Yet the same apostle, writing to the same church later, orders the restoration of a disciplined man lest he be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow. Both letters are in the canon. A church that can do only the severity or only the restoration has half of what was given it, and the half it has will eventually harm someone.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew rabbah meod (H7227), very grievous; shaarurah (H8186), a horrible thing; nebalah (H5039), folly, an outrage; Greek porneia (G4202), fornication.

expand to see more

Hebrew chatathah kabedah meod (H3515) — their sin is very grievous; Genesis 18:20.

Hebrew nebalah (H5039) — folly, an outrage; Judges 19:23–24, 20:6, Genesis 34:7, 2 Samuel 13:12.

Greek porneia (G4202) — fornication; 1 Corinthians 5:1, 6:13, 6:18, Galatians 5:19.

Usage

"“Not so much as named among the Gentiles” — and it was in the church."

"“Ye are puffed up, and have not rather mourned” — the congregation was proud."

"“Consider of it, take advice, and speak your minds” — and the narrator says no more."
